overview: Seeka Limited is one of New Zealand's two largest kiwifruit post-harvest operators, providing an integrated supply chain service from orchard to market across New Zealand and Australia. The company operates 12 packhouse and coolstore facilities covering all major NZ growing regions, owns and leases orchards, and provides retail and wholesale services through its SeekaFresh division. Seeka supplies predominantly to Zespri, the global single-desk kiwifruit marketer; after a softer 2026 harvest versus the FY2025 record, automation-driven margin gains pushed Seeka to a record H1 FY2026 net profit before tax of $62.6m, and management has raised full-year FY2026 guidance twice since, now to $41.0m-$45.0m NPBT.

business_model.summary: Highly seasonal fee-for-service and integrated produce business with approximately 70-90% of gross profit generated in the first half of the calendar year coinciding with the NZ kiwifruit harvest (March-June); H2 typically runs at a loss, pulling full-year NPBT below the H1 figure. Post-harvest operations earn per-tray packing and coolstorage fees from independent growers. Orcharding generates cost-plus margins or profit shares from short and long-term leased orchards that Seeka manages and harvests. SeekaFresh earns commissions on retail sales, wholesale margins, and value-added product revenues. Australian operations are an integrated grower-handler-retailer. The business has strong operating leverage in both directions: FY2024 saw a 44% volume increase drive a 193% EBITDA improvement, FY2025 volumes grew EBITDA a further 26% to a record $96m, and H1 FY2026 showed the inverse can also work in the company's favour - NZ tray volumes fell 4% yet EBITDA still rose 3% and NPBT rose 5% as Reemoon automation lifted post-harvest margins, with the resulting cost efficiency underpinning two consecutive FY2026 guidance increases (from $38-42m in June, to $39-43m in August, to $41-45m in September).
business_model.customer_type: B2B: primarily Zespri (kiwifruit export marketer) and independent NZ growers for post-harvest/orcharding. B2B/B2C: SeekaFresh serves large-format NZ retailers, Asian exporters, and runs a wholesale fresh produce market.
business_model.geographic_mix: New Zealand approximately 92-95% of revenue, Australia approximately 5-8%. NZ operations span Northland (Kerikeri, Orangewood), Coromandel (Peninsula), Bay of Plenty (Katikati, Aongatete, Work Road, Huka Pak, Oakside, KKP, Transpack, OPAC), and Gisborne. Bay of Plenty provides approximately 85% of Seeka's kiwifruit supply.
business_model.seasonality: Highly seasonal - approximately 70-90% of annual gross profit earned in H1 (January-June), with H2 often loss-making. This creates significant working capital requirements during harvest (net bank debt rose from $100.3m at Dec-2025 to $119.8m at June-2026 before falling again post-harvest as receivables are collected) and large period-to-period earnings swings within the year.

main_competitors: EastPack Limited (Te Puke-based co-operative, largest operator ~30% market share)
competitive_position.market_position: Seeka is one of the two largest kiwifruit post-harvest operators in New Zealand alongside EastPack. Seeka packed 47.1 million class 1 trays in the 2025 season (a record) and 45.4 million in the 2026 season, from a total NZ industry Zespri now forecasts at approximately 225 million trays for 2026, representing roughly 20% market share. Seeka is also the largest single kiwifruit grower (by owned/leased hectares managed) in both New Zealand and Australia. It is the only listed pure-play kiwifruit company on the NZX.

moat_factors.factor: Scale and geographic diversification of infrastructure
moat_factors.description: 12 packhouse facilities across all major NZ growing regions (Northland, Coromandel, Bay of Plenty, Gisborne) plus Australian assets. Capacity exceeding 50 million trays. Scale enables investment in automation (Reemoon technology), data visualisation, and grower management tools unattainable by smaller operators. Regional spread reduces single-event weather risk, though the 2026 season showed a broad hot/dry pattern can still compress volumes across regions simultaneously - management nonetheless noted it has spare coolstore capacity it could rent to third parties in 2026.

Seeka's orcharding operations grew approximately 17.5 million class 1 trays in H1 FY2026 (down 8% on pcp's 19.1m, reflecting weaker Hayward yields), representing roughly 40% of the fruit it handles in post-harvest. This vertical integration creates a captive volume base that reduces revenue volatility versus post-harvest-only operators and deepens grower relationships. Long-term lease co-investments with iwi (Raukokore, 70ha) and government agency Kanoa further entrench supply commitments, with new orchards progressively entering full production through the late 2020s.

Multi-year orchard management contracts, a grower loyalty share scheme (shareholders approved issuing up to 1.5 million new shares under the scheme at a special meeting 15 October 2026), and integrated services create switching costs and loyalty. High pre-season grower sign-up rates are highlighted by management as a key metric. The Seeka app provides real-time fruit tracking from NZ packhouse to offshore markets, adding grower value.

New Reemoon kiwifruit packing solutions at Kerikeri and Huka Pak, plus new Reemoon citrus handling automation at Kerikeri, all performed above expectations in their first season (H1 FY2026), lifting post-harvest EBIT 7% to $73.3m despite a 4% decline in total kiwifruit volumes handled. Additional Huka Pak handling automation is scheduled for completion ahead of the 2027 season. Management upgraded guidance twice in 2026 partly on the back of these efficiency gains, elevating this from a 'moderate' to a 'strong' moat factor relative to the prior assessment.

Seeka is an accredited Zespri Registered Supplier with BioGro-certified organic packhouses. These accreditations are necessary to participate in the single-desk export programme and signal quality standards to growers. Seeka's track record of low onshore fruit loss and excellent offshore quality is a competitive differentiator for grower retention.

weaknesses: Revenue is fundamentally volume-driven and highly sensitive to weather, creating binary year-to-year earnings outcomes - illustrated by the June 2026 guidance downgrade following a hotter, drier season, even though cost efficiencies subsequently drove two upward guidance revisions
High fixed-cost base (12 packhouses, coolstores, 600+ permanent staff plus 3,000+ seasonal workers at peak) amplifies earnings volatility when volumes decline
EastPack and other co-operatives can offer growers equity ownership stakes that Seeka, as a public company, cannot match
Concentrated customer: Zespri as single-desk exporter limits pricing leverage on post-harvest service fees

SeekaFresh and Australian businesses remain subscale contributors relative to total capital employed; Australian H1 FY2026 EBIT fell 40% to $2.9m on a hot growing season that reduced average fruit size, again delaying the expected scale-up from new developments

growth_drivers: NZ kiwifruit industry volume growth: Zespri's first full forecast for the 2026 season (as of Sept 2026) projects a record crop of 225 million trays, with per-hectare returns above last year's record in every category except Green and Organic Green (Organic SunGold forecast at $192,000/ha; RubyRed at $117,000/ha). Zespri's January 2026 five-year plan targets 236 million trays by 2030. Seeka's packhouse capacity (>50m trays) is in place to capture its share of industry growth without major additional capital.

SunGold (Gold3) variety shift: SunGold is the premium higher-margin variety with growing per-hectare yields. Seeka packed a record 30.4 million class 1 trays of SunGold in H1 FY2026 (+2% on pcp) even as total Class 1 trays fell to 45.4m, because Hayward (Green) volumes normalised lower (down 13% to 15.0m trays). Continued SunGold mix-shift underpins earnings quality improvement even in a down-volume year.

Post-harvest automation delivering structural cost reduction: all three new Reemoon installations (Kerikeri kiwifruit, Huka Pak kiwifruit, Kerikeri citrus) performed above expectations in their first season, management stated there is further upside as the technology is refined, and additional Huka Pak automation is scheduled ahead of the 2027 season. This is Seeka's primary driver of the two FY2026 guidance upgrades since June.

Orchard development pipeline entering production: 70+ hectares co-developed with iwi in Raukokore, plus ongoing investment in kiwifruit and avocado on long-term leased land. These orchards will progressively increase Seeka's captive volume supply through the late 2020s, though the pace of ramp can be masked in any single hot/dry season.

Australian business scale-up from new developments: continued investment in kiwifruit, European pears, nashi, jujube and the new Ruby Roo red nashi variety. Expected production growth did not materialise in H1 FY2026 due to a hot growing season (kiwifruit tonnage flat at 2,226 tonnes, other fruit down sharply), but Seeka is adapting orchard management (carrying lower fruit numbers for size) and new heat-tolerant varieties, pushing the anticipated earnings lift further into future seasons.

Debt reduction and balance sheet resilience: net bank debt fell from $172m (2023 peak) to $137.3m (Dec 2024) to $100.3m (Dec 2025); the June 2026 seasonal build to $119.8m was still $10.8m below June 2025, with the leverage ratio improving to 1.22x (well below the covenant target range) from 1.60x a year earlier. Seeka also renewed its banking syndicate and reduced total facility size by $20m to $184m, reflecting reduced funding need. Lower interest costs ($3.6m in H1 FY2026 vs $5.0m pcp) are flowing through to after-tax returns.

Grower loyalty share scheme renewal: shareholders approved (15 October 2026 special meeting) issuing up to 1.5 million new shares under the scheme, reinforcing grower retention and alignment without a cash cost.

Supplementary packing categories and diversification: citrus, persimmon, kiwiberry and avocado packing use packhouse capacity during off-peak kiwifruit periods. SeekaFresh's LUVO oil (avocado, olive, macadamia, coconut, following the 2025 Olivado asset purchase and new Northland manufacturing facility) is starting to achieve market success, with Retail Services EBIT up 39% to $1.4m in H1 FY2026.

business.description: Kiwifruit yields are highly sensitive to growing conditions. Seeka's annual EBITDA has ranged from $26m (FY2023, Cyclone Gabrielle and drought) to $96m (FY2025, record volumes). The 2026 season volumes fell on a hotter, drier growing season, though automation efficiency gains meant H1 FY2026 EBITDA still rose 3% despite the 4% volume decline - demonstrating some, but not complete, insulation from weather swings. The Bay of Plenty provides approximately 85% of Seeka's kiwifruit supply, creating geographic concentration risk.

The large majority of Seeka's revenue is generated through the Zespri system. Zespri holds the mandated single-desk export licence under NZ Kiwifruit Export Regulations. Any regulatory change removing or weakening this mandate, changes to Zespri's pool allocation methodology, or shifts in Zespri's service fee expectations would directly impact Seeka. Seeka has limited negotiating leverage with Zespri given its scale advantage, though Zespri's September 2026 forecast of record per-hectare returns across most categories for the 2026 crop is a near-term tailwind for grower (and indirectly Seeka) economics.

business.risk: Grower retention and competition for supply
business.description: EastPack and other co-operative operators can offer growers equity ownership that Seeka cannot as a public company. Pre-season grower signup rates are a critical operational metric. Loss of significant grower supply to competitors reduces volumes and increases per-unit fixed costs disproportionately. Seeka's October 2026 grower loyalty share scheme renewal is a direct response to this competitive pressure.

Psa-V bacterial canker has been endemic in NZ kiwifruit since 2010 and remains a persistent yield and vine health risk. The SunGold Gold3 variety has better Psa tolerance but is not immune. A new virulent Psa strain or adverse weather creating conditions favourable to Psa proliferation could impact vine productivity across Seeka's growing and post-harvest network. Australian operations are also Psa-affected, with an ongoing crop protection programme.

The high fixed-cost structure (packhouses, coolstores, permanent workforce) means a reduction in volumes can create a disproportionate EBITDA/NPBT swing, though the H1 FY2026 result (NPBT +5% on volumes -4%) shows automation has partially decoupled earnings from raw tray counts in a moderate downturn. A severe weather event (a repeat of FY2023-level volumes, ~30m trays) would likely still produce a pre-tax loss. This binary earnings profile at the extremes remains the fundamental investment risk in the stock.

financial.description: Net bank debt of $119.8m at June 2026 (leverage ratio 1.22x, down from 1.60x a year earlier and well below the covenant target range). Seeka required covenant waivers in mid-2023 following Cyclone Gabrielle crop losses, but headroom is now comfortable; the banking syndicate was renewed and total facility size reduced by $20m to $184m in 2026, reflecting reduced funding need. Downgraded from 'moderate' given the sustained deleveraging trend and syndicate renewal.

The seasonal business requires significant working capital to fund harvest operations, packhouse costs, and grower advance programmes in H1 before cash is collected from Zespri later in the season. Net bank debt rose from $100.3m (Dec 2025) to $119.8m (June 2026) to fund the harvest, before Seeka banked $55.0m in July 2026 as receivables were collected, in line with normal seasonal cash flow. Trade and other receivables were $116.7m at June 2026.

The 2024 NZ legislation removing tax deductibility of building depreciation created a one-off non-cash deferred tax charge in FY2024 and increased total deferred tax liabilities ($50.9m at June 2026). This creates an ongoing wedge between NPBT and reported NPAT, though H1 FY2026 NPAT still grew faster (+20%) than NPBT (+5%) due to a lower deferred tax charge versus pcp.

Australian operations (~5-8% of revenue) are conducted in AUD creating translation risk. Some USD exposure exists through Zespri's export pricing. Currency movements are secondary in magnitude to volume and operating risks.

regulatory.description: Seeka provides seasonal work and pastoral care to more than 1,200 RSE (Recognised Seasonal Employee) workers from Pacific nations, alongside 600+ permanent staff and 3,000+ total seasonal workers at peak harvest. RSE scheme quotas, immigration policy, and Accredited Employer Work Visa conditions directly affect labour availability and cost during the critical harvest window.

Zespri's export monopoly is granted under NZ Kiwifruit Export Regulations and periodically comes under review. Any change to the regulatory framework would restructure the kiwifruit supply chain and could fundamentally alter grower-packhouse commercial relationships.

NZ IFRS 18 Presentation and Disclosure in Financial Statements becomes effective for periods beginning on or after 1 January 2027, replacing NZ IAS 1. Seeka disclosed in its H1 FY2026 interim report that the standard will change the layout of the income statement, cash flow statement and require new management-defined performance measure (MPM) disclosures (e.g., reconciling EBITDA to operating profit), but management expects no change to net profit before tax, cash, or cash equivalents - a presentation rather than economic change.

Seeka is subject to XRB's NZ Climate Standards NZ CS 1-3. Seeka's 2026 Sustainability Report confirmed a 30% reduction in Scope 1 and 2 greenhouse gas emissions from the 2022 baseline, with a new target of 50% reduction by 2030, achieved via refrigerant switching, fleet electrification (18% of fleet electric/hybrid), solar installation (1,165 kW across five facilities) and biowaste diversion.

International market access for NZ kiwifruit depends on phytosanitary standards managed by MPI and Zespri. Any new biosecurity detections, pest incursions, or quality failures could trigger market access restrictions affecting the entire industry supply chain.

macro.risk: Climate change and extreme weather events
macro.description: The 2023 season was severely impacted by Cyclone Gabrielle, and the 2026 season was hit by a hotter and drier than usual growing season in both New Zealand and Australia, reducing volumes. Climate research indicates the core Bay of Plenty growing region may face increasing production challenges from changing weather patterns including reduced winter chill, increased drought frequency, and more intense cyclonic events. Management noted 2026 winter chill was good, lifting the probability of a strong 2027 season, but cautioned it is too early to make a reliable prediction. Seeka is responding with regional diversification, orchard management changes (e.g., Australian fruit-thinning for size), and new heat-tolerant varieties, but cannot fully mitigate systemic weather risk.

macro.risk: Global kiwifruit market pricing and Northern Hemisphere competition
macro.description: Zespri's September 2026 forecast for the 2026 crop points to record per-hectare returns in most categories, a positive near-term signal, but Zespri's global licensing programme has expanded SunGold production in Italy, France and other Northern Hemisphere markets, which will eventually create more supply competition for the NZ-grown premium. Unauthorized Chinese SunGold production also dilutes variety positioning, though Zespri has been winning legal battles against it.

Management continues to flag higher input costs (labour, electricity, packaging) as an ongoing challenge in the H1 FY2026 result, even as automation investment helped more than offset these pressures on a net margin basis in the period.

execution.description: Seeka has committed capital to new Australian orchard developments (kiwifruit, pear, jujube, and the Ruby Roo nashi variety) intended to lift Australian earnings. For the second consecutive period, expected production growth did not materialise - H1 FY2026 kiwifruit tonnage was flat and EBIT fell 40% to $2.9m due to a hot growing season reducing fruit size. Achieving acceptable returns on invested capital requires successful Psa management, crop quality improvement, and market development in a geography where Seeka lacks its NZ scale advantages.

The Reemoon technology installations at Kerikeri and Huka Pak (kiwifruit) and Kerikeri (citrus) performed above expectations in their first season (H1 FY2026), a positive early validation that reduces this risk relative to prior assessments. Additional Huka Pak handling automation is scheduled ahead of the 2027 season; continued commissioning and optimisation risk remains but the track record to date is encouraging.

Chair Mark Dewdney and director Hayley Gourley (both appointed within the prior 12-18 months) have overseen a volatile guidance period in 2026 (initial cut, then two consecutive raises) and the October 2026 grower loyalty share scheme renewal. Governance continuity appears sound given CEO Michael Franks' operational continuity through the period.

macro_factors.industry_outlook: The NZ kiwifruit industry remains in a structural growth phase. Zespri's first full forecast for the 2026 season (as of September 2026) projects a record crop of approximately 225 million trays, with per-hectare returns above last year's record in nearly every category (Organic SunGold ~$192,000/ha; RubyRed ~$117,000/ha), driven by strong North American demand and encouraging signs in Europe. Zespri's January 2026 five-year outlook targets 236 million trays by 2030 (from 214 million in 2025), with SunGold projected to grow 17% to 163.5m trays and RubyRed more than doubling; up to 400 hectares of new SunGold licences are being released in 2026. The key uncertainty remains the competitive impact of Northern Hemisphere licensed SunGold production (Italy, France) on per-tray returns over the 5-10 year horizon.
macro_factors.cyclicality: High operational cyclicality within years (H1-heavy with 70-90% of annual gross profit, H2 often loss-making) and meaningful year-to-year swings driven by harvest volumes, though H1 FY2026 showed automation can partially decouple earnings from volume in a moderate (non-crisis) down season. Seeka's annual EBITDA has ranged from $26m (FY2023) to $96m (FY2025). Unlike typical agriculture, the industry benefits from Zespri's single-desk coordination which provides some demand-side stability through premium market management even when volumes vary.
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Moderate. Net bank debt of $119.8m at June 2026 (seasonally elevated from $100.3m at Dec 2025) on a variable-rate facility means NZ OCR movements directly affect interest expenses. Interest costs fell to $3.6m in H1 FY2026 from $5.0m in the pcp as both debt levels and rates declined, a tailwind that has supported the 2026 guidance upgrades.
key_input_costs: Labour: largest cost driver - 600+ permanent staff plus 1,200+ RSE seasonal workers and up to 3,000 total seasonal workers at harvest peak.

Electricity: powers packhouses and coolstores, a major operating expense subject to NZ electricity market pricing. Seeka continues to invest in solar (1,165 kW installed across five facilities) and natural refrigerants to manage this exposure.
Packaging materials: trays, cartons, labels scale directly with volumes. Inflationary pressures noted by management as an ongoing cost challenge, partially offset by automation efficiency gains.
Refrigerants: transitioning to environmentally friendly refrigerants to reduce both operational costs, leak risk, and emissions, contributing to a 30% GHG reduction from the 2022 baseline.
Fuel: transport fleet for orchard-to-packhouse logistics and outbound distribution; 18% of the fleet is now electric or hybrid.

recent_developments.event: Special shareholder meeting passed the ordinary resolution authorising Seeka to issue up to 1.5 million new ordinary shares under its Grower Loyalty Share Scheme, renewing a mechanism that has run since 2019 to help retain grower supply.
The $0.20/share fully imputed interim dividend (declared 19 August 2026, record date 18 September 2026) was paid; dividend reinvestment plan allotment completed 14 October 2026.

Seeka raised full-year FY2026 NPBT guidance a second time, to $41.0m-$45.0m (from $39.0m-$43.0m set in August), citing continued strength from post-harvest automation and cost management. This compares with FY2025 actual NPBT of $47.5m.

Zespri issued its first full forecast for the 2026 kiwifruit season: a record crop of approximately 225 million trays, with per-hectare returns above the prior year's record in nearly every category except Green and Organic Green, driven by strong North American demand.

H1 FY2026 interim result (six months to 30 June 2026): Revenue $305.5m (-1%), EBITDA $86.3m (+3%), EBIT $69.7m (+4%), record NPBT $62.6m (+5%), NPAT $45.4m (+20%). NZ Class 1 trays packed 45.4m (-4% vs pcp's record 47.1m); SunGold record 30.4m trays (+2%), Hayward down 13% to 15.0m. Post-harvest EBIT +7% to $73.3m on automation efficiency gains; Orcharding EBIT -20% to $6.3m on lower Hayward yields; Retail Services (SeekaFresh) EBIT +39% to $1.4m; Australia EBIT -40% to $2.9m on a hot growing season. Net bank debt $119.8m (down $10.8m YoY), leverage ratio improved to 1.22x from 1.60x. Banking syndicate renewed with facility reduced $20m to $184m. Full-year NPBT guidance raised to $39.0m-$43.0m from the June $38.0m-$42.0m. Declared $0.20/share dividend; management flagged intent to revert to a twice-yearly dividend cadence (considered August/February, paid October/April).

First FY2026 earnings guidance issued alongside confirmation of the completed 2026 kiwifruit harvest: NPBT guided to $38.0m-$42.0m, down from FY2025's $47.5m. NZ Class 1 tray volumes 45.4 million (down from the 2025 record of 47.1 million); record SunGold volume offset by lower, more normal Hayward (Green) yields. Australian kiwifruit harvest fell on a hotter, drier growing season, meaning expected production growth from new Australian orchard developments did not materialise in 2026.
Seeka released its 2026 Sustainability Report: confirmed a 30% reduction in Scope 1 and 2 GHG emissions from the 2022 baseline, with a new target of 50% reduction by 2030.

FY2025 annual result released (year ended 31 December 2025): Revenue $439.6m (+7%), EBITDA $95.9m (+26%), EBIT $62.6m (+34%), NPBT $47.5m (+60%), NPAT $32.0m (+265% reported), EPS $0.76. Net bank debt $100.3m, down 27% from $137.3m. Post-harvest packed record 47.1m class 1 trays (+10%). Board acknowledged it was 'too early to reliably indicate 2026,' noting positive early winter chill indicators that did not fully translate into a repeat record season due to a subsequent hot, dry spring/summer.

Seeka purchased the assets of Olivado, resetting SeekaFresh's avocado oil manufacturing and marketing business under the LUVO oil brand (avocado, olive, macadamia, coconut), including a new Northland manufacturing facility; LUVO is now starting to achieve market success per the H1 FY2026 update.

guidance.management_commentary: Management's August 2026 interim commentary described the record H1 result as driven by automation efficiency gains (Reemoon technology at Kerikeri, Huka Pak, and new citrus handling) outperforming forecast in their first season, more than offsetting a 4% decline in NZ kiwifruit volumes and higher input costs. Management stated it is too early to make a reliable prediction on the 2027 crop, but noted good 2026 winter chill improves the odds of a strong 2027 season. The company reiterated it has spare post-harvest capacity and systems to handle higher future NZ kiwifruit volumes and is evaluating future capacity and growth opportunities. The subsequent 16 September 2026 announcement raised guidance again without extensive qualitative commentary beyond continued automation/cost-management strength.

bull_case: Earnings resilience through a down-volume season: H1 FY2026 NPBT grew 5% and NPAT grew 20% even as NZ kiwifruit trays fell 4%, and management has raised full-year guidance twice since the initial June 2026 cut (now $41-45m NPBT), evidencing that FY2024-25's recovery reflects durable structural improvement (automation, cost discipline, debt reduction) rather than a weather-driven spike that fully reverses in a softer year.

Automation investment cycle validated: all three new Reemoon installations (Kerikeri kiwifruit and citrus, Huka Pak kiwifruit) performed above expectations in their first season, with further Huka Pak automation scheduled ahead of 2027 and management flagging additional performance upside as the technology is refined - a credible, now-proven driver of structural margin expansion.

Powerful industry tailwinds with capacity already in place: Zespri's September 2026 forecast points to a record 225 million-tray 2026 crop with record per-hectare returns in nearly every category, and its five-year plan targets 236 million trays by 2030. Seeka's >50m tray post-harvest capacity is in place without requiring major additional capital, so continued industry growth flows through at high incremental margins.

Balance sheet materially de-risked and capital returns resuming: net bank debt down from $172m (2023 peak) to $119.8m (June 2026, seasonally elevated) with leverage at 1.22x (well below covenant targets, improved from 1.60x a year earlier); banking syndicate renewed with a smaller facility. Seeka paid $0.20/share in October 2026 and signalled a return to a twice-yearly dividend cadence, underscoring confidence in sustained profitability.

Grower loyalty mechanism renewed: the October 2026 shareholder approval to issue up to 1.5 million shares under the Grower Loyalty Share Scheme reinforces Seeka's ability to retain supply against co-operative competitors without cash cost, supporting the volume base underlying all other growth drivers.
bear_case: Earnings remain fundamentally volume- and weather-sensitive: a routine hot, dry season in 2026 (not a cyclone-scale event) was still enough to cut NZ kiwifruit volumes 4% and knock down the initial guidance range materially versus FY2025's record, and it hit New Zealand and Australia simultaneously (Australian H1 EBIT -40%), undermining the geographic-diversification thesis even though subsequent cost performance partly offset the hit.

Fundamental Zespri concentration and single-desk risk: the large majority of Seeka's revenue flows through the Zespri system. Seeka cannot independently market kiwifruit internationally and has limited pricing power on post-harvest service fees. Any regulatory change to the single-desk structure or deterioration in Zespri's global market performance would directly harm Seeka with no alternative outlets.

Australian expansion returns delayed for a second consecutive period: expected production growth from new Australian orchard developments (kiwifruit, pear, jujube, Ruby Roo nashi) again did not materialise in H1 FY2026 due to adverse weather, with EBIT down 40%, raising questions about the payback timeline on this capital.

Analyst sentiment has been skeptical: as of early October 2026, aggregate analyst price targets (median ~NZ$2.55 across covering analysts, with none rating the stock a buy) sat well below the prevailing share price (~NZ$5.18-5.20), and a key broker (Jarden) has previously cut its target with an underweight rating - suggesting the market/stock price may be running ahead of consensus fundamental views even after the guidance upgrades.

Wide historical earnings range and valuation risk: annual NPBT has ranged from roughly a $21m pre-tax loss (FY2023) to $47.5m (FY2025); even with two 2026 guidance upgrades, full-year NPBT guidance of $41-45m would still fall short of the FY2025 record, and a severe weather event in a future season (a repeat of FY2023-level conditions) would again test covenant headroom and dividend sustainability.

Northern Hemisphere SunGold competition emerging: Zespri's global licensing programme has expanded SunGold production across Italy, France and other Northern Hemisphere growers. While currently complementary to NZ supply (different seasons), increasing licensed Northern Hemisphere volumes will eventually put pressure on the price premium earned for NZ-grown SunGold as total global supply rises faster than demand.
